sentence: However, existing models—such as GANs, VAEs, and diffusion networks—often struggle to jointly achieve high fidelity, fairness, and generalization, particularly in complex, imbalanced, or multimodal domains.

Despite these advances, ensuring both fidelity and fairness in synthetic data remains a major hurdle, especially in high-dimensional or multimodal domains such as network traffic or clinical decision-making.

Conceptual Overview The Hybrid Fairness-Aware Generative Model (HFAGM++) addresses the problem of achieving robust, fair, and generalizable learning in data-scarce and bias-prone domains such as clinical diagnostics or multimodal behavioral analytics.

Experiments and Experimental Settings The experiments were designed to empirically validate the theoretical constructs introduced in Section 3 by testing HFAGM++ under fairness-critical, data-scarce, and multimodal conditions.

To comprehensively evaluate fairness , generalization , and cross-modal transferability , three data regimes were employed: structured biomedical data, temporal-visual sign language data, and a cross-domain transfer scenario linking both modalities.
Together, they provide a rigorous multimodal benchmark for assessing the scalability and theoretical validity of HFAGM++.
These datasets consist of RGB video sequences (224 × 224 pixels) depicting isolated Arabic signs performed by multiple signers.
Unlike baseline fairness methods, which degrade sharply when transferred across modalities, HFAGM++ maintains bounded DPD/EOD (≤ 0.38) in the ArSL → COVID transfer.
HFAGM++ encloses the smallest fairness gap region and attains the highest utility, confirming improved geometric stability and fairness preservation across modalities.

Results The experimental evaluation of the Hybrid Fairness-Aware Generative Model (HFAGM++) was conducted to validate the theoretical foundations presented in Section 3 and to assess empirical robustness under fairness-critical, multimodal, and cross-domain conditions.

This consistency across modalities demonstrates that fairness is encoded geometrically in the latent space rather than as an after-the-fact correction at the prediction level.

The fine-tuned ArSL encoder retained its equitable latent structure when transferred to clinical prediction, proving that fairness geometry generalizes across modalities—a key novelty distinguishing HFAGM++ from domain-specific fairness methods.

Together, they demonstrate that HFAGM++ sustains high predictive utility (AUC ≈ 0.95–0.99) while maintaining bounded fairness deviations across recursive generations and under cross-modality adaptation.

This unified set of results confirms the dual strengths of HFAGM++: (1) high-fidelity fairness regularization that generalizes across data modalities, and (2) bounded-drift stability ensuring reproducible fairness geometry under recursive synthesis and cross-domain transfer.

Discussion and Comparative Evaluation The three experiments collectively confirm that the proposed Hybrid Fairness-Aware Generative Model (HFAGM++) establishes a reproducible, theoretically grounded, and empirically stable framework for fairness-aware learning across structured and multimodal domains.
Experiment 2 (ArSL Visual Data) extended this validation to a temporal-visual modality.
This demonstrates that HFAGM++ sustains fair geometry across modalities—a property rarely verified in fairness research.
The results imply that fairness-aware recursion can serve as a general framework for equitable synthetic data generation in biomedical and multimodal applications.

Conclusion This study presented the Hybrid Fairness-Aware Generative Model (HFAGM++) , a unified framework designed to achieve fairness-preserving generalization across structured and multimodal data.
Moreover, the cross-domain transfer experiment established that HFAGM++ generalizes fairness across modality boundaries, achieving robustness under distributional shifts.
